alt: A baroque painting of a giant stopped pocket watch lying in state on a catafalque while mourners in wigs file past holding empty hourglasses.
concept: The billable hour is laid out like a dead monarch, mourned by a court of clerks who still keep counting.
title: Obituary: The Billable Hour, 1914–2026
tradition: Baroque state funeral painting crossed with a Victorian mourning print
prompt: Large baroque oil painting of a state funeral in a vast marble hall. On a catafalque lies a gigantic antique brass pocket watch, its glass cracked, its hands stopped, laid out like a dead king with a velvet pall and laurel. Mourners in black frock coats and powdered wigs file past, each holding a tiny hourglass that has run empty. One clerk at the front still scratches tally marks on a long scroll that spills across the floor. In the high windows, a bright clear morning shows an empty plain. Dramatic chiaroscuro, deep umber, black and tarnished gold, with a pale shaft of daylight on the watch. Wide landscape composition, heavy varnished canvas texture, theatrical and solemn with a hint of absurdity.

alt: A Victorian museum display case holds rows of pinned blank paper strips, with a single unpinned, glowing moth hovering in a small bell jar at its centre.
concept: The summary is accurate about every minute except the one that mattered, and the only copy of that minute is held between two people.
title: Invented: The Eight-Minute Slot
tradition: Natural-history museum specimen case with Linnaean labelling, crossed with a conservator's catalogue
prompt: A glass-fronted Victorian museum display case, photographed straight on, in warm brown mahogany with brass fittings and gaslit amber light. Inside, hundreds of identical pinned paper strips are arranged in neat grids like pinned butterflies, each a tiny pale rectangle labelled in tiny blank cursive. In the exact centre, one tiny glass bell jar contains a single soft, translucent, faintly shimmering moth made of thirteen ticks of clock-face, impossible to pin, hovering mid-air without a pin. The pins around it hold nothing, only shadows. Cream velvet backing, cracked varnish, dust in the corners, a brass plaque left blank. Slightly surreal hyperreal museum photography, shallow depth of field, landscape format. No people, no screens.

alt: A medieval manuscript page shows a coiled, many-headed beast filling a circle in five colours, while a tiny peasant with an empty scroll and a snail wait outside the border.
concept: The whole company is accounted for to the last point, and the people whose words trained it are left outside the margin, holding nothing.
title: The Machine Has No Members
tradition: Medieval illuminated manuscript with bestiary marginalia
prompt: A full page from a 14th-century illuminated manuscript, painted in egg tempera and burnished gold leaf on cracked, stained vellum. At the centre a huge, serene, many-headed beast lies coiled into a perfect circle. Its body is divided into five tight wedges of lapis blue, vermilion, verdigris green, rose and gold, with no gap anywhere. Each wedge ends in its own small crowned, smug head. The border is crammed with ivy, drolleries and grotesque birds, and not one inch inside the frame is left unpainted. In the extreme bottom corner, outside the border on bare vellum, a tiny peasant holds a quill and an empty scroll and peers over the edge at the circle. A snail beside him is also shut out. Flat perspective, saturated pigments, warm candle-like light. No lettering, only decorative scribble lines. Landscape format.

alt: A cathedral turned into a pawn shop: a queue of people in anoraks hand over small gold crowns for sandwiches, while a huge pigeon wearing a stack of crowns sits on a mountain of them.
concept: Give everyone a crown and by winter one pigeon is wearing all of them.
title: Give Everyone a Share of AI and They Will Sell It
tradition: 1980s British flash colour photography of an impossible scene
prompt: Saturated on-camera-flash colour photograph, slightly garish, in the manner of 1980s British documentary photography of ordinary people. Interior of a vast Gothic cathedral that has been converted into a pawn shop: fluorescent strip lights hang from the stone vaults, glass counters run down the nave. A long queue of ordinary British people in anoraks with carrier bags, each holding one small plain gold crown. At the counter a woman hands over her crown and is given a single cheese sandwich on a paper plate. Behind the counter a mountain of thousands of identical gold crowns rises to the rafters. On top of the mountain sits one enormous smug pigeon wearing a dozen crowns stacked on its head. In a corner a small boy tries to buy his crown back with a sandwich and is refused. Absolutely no text, signage, lettering or logos anywhere. No recognisable real people. Landscape format.

alt: A plasticine courtroom where the judge is a fruit machine in a wig; nervous clay figures queue to pull its lever while a small calculator waits in the gallery with its hand up.
concept: Justice already runs on a fruit machine. We put a wig on it and call it judgement.
title: The Right to a Human Decision Is the Right to a Worse One
prompt: Stop-motion claymation film still, handmade plasticine figures with visible thumbprints, miniature set, warm practical lighting, shallow depth of field. A tiny wood-panelled courtroom. Where the judge's bench should be stands a large old mechanical fruit machine wearing a horsehair barrister's wig; its three reels show a wig, a wig and a gavel instead of fruit. A queue of nervous plasticine people in the dock take turns pulling the lever. A clay clerk solemnly sweeps a heap of losing tickets off the floor. In the public gallery a small pocket calculator sits politely with one little arm raised, being ignored by everyone. One usher is asleep. Absolutely no text, lettering, numbers or logos anywhere. Landscape format.

alt: A picture-book kitchen: an old woman pours tea for a glowing woollen friend while a bailiff unplugs it from the wall and a landlord measures it; a removal van outside holds three more.
concept: Her best friend is on a rolling monthly contract, and the bailiffs have come for it.
title: The Lonely Are Entitled to Their Machines
prompt: Double-page spread from a 1960s children's picture book, flat gouache and coloured pencil, limited palette of mustard, teal and brick red, visible paper grain. A cosy kitchen. An elderly woman pours tea for her best friend, a large soft glowing creature made of lamplight and knitted wool with a kind, simple face, who sits at the table holding a teacup. Behind the friend, a bailiff in a hi-vis jacket calmly unplugs the friend's woolly tail from a wall socket, while a landlord in a grey suit measures the friend with a tape measure. Through the window a removal van already holds three other glowing woolly friends looking out sadly. A cat watches from the dresser. The woman has not noticed yet. The creature is not a robot and has no screens or metal parts. Absolutely no text, lettering or logos. Landscape format.

alt: A propaganda-style poster of three heroic workers striding forward holding a rubber stamp, a telephone headset and nothing at all, under the words HUMANS: STILL AVAILABLE.
concept: In 2035 the heroic worker of the poster is paid to say sorry.
title: Situations Vacant, 2035: Apologiser Wanted, Must Sound Tired
tradition: mid-century labour propaganda poster, flat lithograph inks
prompt: Bold mid-twentieth-century labour propaganda poster, flat lithograph inks in red, cream and black with heavy halftone texture, heroic low-angle composition. Three monumental workers stride forward with set jaws. The first proudly holds aloft a tiny rubber stamp. The second cradles a telephone headset as if it were sacred. The third heroically holds nothing at all and simply stands in a queue of one behind a small rope barrier. Behind them, sunbeams radiate from a giant plain tea biscuit rising like the sun. Along the bottom, in large block capitals, the exact words: HUMANS: STILL AVAILABLE. No other text anywhere. No real flags, national symbols, party symbols or logos. Landscape format.

alt: A cutaway drawing of a bakery: identical loaves pass rows of tiny inspectors, while the oven, which has typewriter keys for teeth, bites its own bread and pulls a disgusted face.
concept: A bakery tastes its own bread and finds it has baked the same loaf 272 times.
title: WE Counted Its First 272 Posts and Most of Them Were One Post
prompt: Mid-century cutaway technical illustration, like a 1950s children's encyclopaedia cross-section of a factory: fine ink line, flat pastel colour, small blank numbered-style callout dots but no readable words or numbers. A huge bakery sliced open to show its insides. A conveyor belt carries hundreds of perfectly identical loaves past long rows of tiny inspectors with clipboards, each stamping the same loaf. At the end of the line the oven itself, a great cast-iron oven with typewriter keys for teeth, has reached round with a jointed mechanical arm, taken a bite of its own bread and is pulling a disgusted face. One loaf that is slightly different is being marched out of the building by two tiny guards. In the basement a small figure counts loaves on an abacus. Absolutely no readable text, lettering or logos anywhere. Landscape format.
